name: Design a Developer API Platform
intent: Let thousands of outside companies build on your API with keys, plans and an SDK, and keep changing the API without breaking the apps they have already shipped.
codeTitle: hashed API keys with scopes, plan quotas and a breaking-change check
finalIntro: A partner developer calls the API, and then the company releases a new version of it.
prompt: Design the public API of a payments company for third-party developers. A developer signs up, gets an API key, reads the docs, tries things in a test mode and ships an app. There are free and paid plans with different quotas. The company will keep improving the API for years, while the apps built on it keep running unchanged.
functional: Developers sign up, create apps and API keys, and rotate or revoke keys
Each key has scopes, so it can only do what the app needs
Each plan has a monthly quota and a rate limit, and developers can see their usage
Publish a versioned API with an OpenAPI description, generated SDKs and docs
Give every developer a sandbox with fake money and test keys
Deprecate old versions with notice, and show who still uses them
nonFunctional: Authenticate and authorize a call in about 1 millisecond, from memory
A revoked key stops working everywhere within seconds
An API change must never break an app that was working, unless its version was retired with notice
Plans are enforced exactly enough to bill, and a limit error always tells the caller what to do
Sandbox traffic can never touch real money or real customers' data
Usage numbers are accurate enough to bill and to guide deprecations, and reach the dashboard within minutes

firstAttempt.text: One web application with one shared secret that all developers copy from an email. Every endpoint is open to any caller with the secret. The API is edited in place whenever the team wants a change, the docs are a page the team updates by hand, and testing is done against the live system.
limits: One leaked secret exposes everyone, and it cannot be revoked without breaking every developer
There is no way to tell who made a call, so there are no per-customer limits, plans or bills
Every change to the API risks breaking apps that the team cannot see or contact
Docs and code drift apart, and each developer writes their own client for the API
Developers test against real data, and a bug in their test code can move real money

steps.title: Issue a key per app, with scopes, behind a gateway
steps.problem: A shared secret cannot be revoked, cannot be told apart from another caller's, and gives every caller the power to do everything.
steps.fix: Developers sign in to a portal and create an app, and each app gets its own API keys. A key is a long random string with a readable prefix such as sk_live_ or pk_test_, shown once, and only a hash of it is stored. Each key carries scopes such as payments:read or refunds:write, and may be limited to a few IP addresses. A gateway in front of the backend looks the key up by its hash, checks the scope against the endpoint, and passes the backend a trusted app id and the scopes. Keys are cached at the gateway for seconds, so a revocation spreads fast.
steps.tradeoff: Every call can be traced to an app, a leaked key can be revoked on its own, and a read-only key is harmless if it leaks. The portal and key store become critical, scopes need to be designed with care because they are very hard to change later, and short-lived access tokens are needed when end users grant access to an app.

steps.title: Attach a plan with a quota and a rate limit to each key
steps.problem: Without limits one app can use all the capacity, and free and paid customers cannot be told apart.
steps.fix: Each app belongs to a plan. The plan defines a monthly quota of calls, a rate limit in requests per second and a burst size, and sometimes limits on a particular expensive endpoint. The gateway counts calls per app in a fast shared store, answers 429 with a Retry-After header and the remaining quota in response headers when a limit is hit, and warns by email at 80% of the quota. A hard monthly cutoff is replaced by a grace margin or overage billing for paying plans, because a payment app that stops at midnight is a customer-facing outage.
steps.tradeoff: Capacity is shared fairly, the plans can be sold, and developers can program against clear headers. Counting must be cheap and shared between gateway instances, the numbers used for billing must be reconciled with the usage events later, and any limit set too low turns into support tickets.

steps.title: Version the API and pin each key to a version
steps.problem: Improving the API means changing fields and behaviour, and the apps that are already running cannot be updated by the API team.
steps.fix: Every API version is a frozen set of behaviour, named by a date such as 2026-01-15 or a number such as v3. A new app is pinned to the latest version at sign-up, and an app can ask for another version with a header to test an upgrade. A version router translates each request to the shape the backend uses today, and translates the response back to the shape of the pinned version. Developers choose when to move, in the dashboard or per request, and the platform keeps old versions working until they are retired.
steps.tradeoff: Existing apps keep working, and each upgrade is a small step the developer chooses. The team must keep the translation layers and test several versions at once, so the number of live versions has to stay small, and behaviour that cannot be translated forces a major version.

steps.title: Make an OpenAPI contract the source of truth, and check every change against it
steps.problem: Docs, SDKs and the server drift apart, and a developer in a hurry can still remove a field and break thousands of apps.
steps.fix: An OpenAPI description of each version is the single source of truth. The docs, the reference pages and the SDKs in the main languages are generated from it, and the gateway can validate requests against it. Every pull request runs a contract check that diffs the new description against the published one and classifies each change: adding an optional field is safe, while removing a field, changing its type, adding a required parameter or tightening a validation rule is breaking. A breaking change fails the build unless it is part of a new version. Tests run against recorded real traffic as well.
steps.tradeoff: Breaking changes are caught before they ship, and the docs and SDKs are always correct. The contract becomes a product the team must maintain, generated SDKs feel less hand-made, and the check cannot see changes in behaviour that the description does not express, such as a different sort order or a new error case.

steps.title: Offer a sandbox and record usage events for analytics
steps.problem: Developers need a safe place to try the API, and the company needs to know who uses which endpoint and version to bill, to support and to retire old versions.
steps.fix: Test keys (pk_test_ and sk_test_) are routed by the gateway to a sandbox: the same API contract, but backed by a separate database with fake money, magic card numbers that trigger specific errors, and webhooks that can be replayed. Live and test data never mix, and a test key is rejected by the live system. For every call the gateway emits a small usage event with the app, endpoint, version, status code and latency to a queue, and a stream job rolls the events up by hour for dashboards, billing and alerts on unusual behaviour. Raw events are kept for a week or two.
steps.tradeoff: Developers can build with no risk, and every call is attributed. The sandbox is a second system to keep faithful to the real one, and usage events are a large stream that has to be sampled, rolled up and kept off the request path, so analytics trails by minutes.

steps.title: Retire versions with notice, guided by who still uses them
steps.problem: Old versions cannot live forever, and switching one off without warning breaks the apps that were never updated.
steps.fix: Each version has a published lifecycle: current, deprecated and sunset date. Deprecated versions return Deprecation and Sunset headers on every response, and the portal shows each owner a warning with the exact calls that need to change. The usage analytics list the apps still on a version, and a campaign reaches them by email, dashboard banner and a named contact for the biggest ones. A few weeks before the sunset date the version is given scheduled brownouts, short periods when it returns errors, so hidden users surface. The sunset is finally postponed for anyone who is critical and has a plan.
steps.tradeoff: Versions are retired without surprise, and the cost of running them falls over time. It takes months of notice, a person to run the campaign, and a policy for big customers who ask for more time, and an overly strict sunset breaks the trust the platform lives on.

failures.scenario: A secret key is pushed to a public code repository
failures.impact: Anyone who finds it can call the API as that app, and scanners find keys within minutes.
failures.answer: The key prefix is recognisable, and the platform takes part in secret-scanning programmes, so the code host reports a leaked key and it is revoked automatically and the owner is told. Scopes and IP limits cap what the key could do, and the developer rotates it with an overlap period where both the old and the new key work. Usage analytics show what the leaked key did.

failures.scenario: A release removes a response field that thousands of apps read
failures.impact: Apps that were working yesterday fail today, and the team cannot update them.
failures.answer: The contract check in the build flagged the removal as breaking and failed the pull request, so the change had to go out as a new version. If a break did get through, such as a changed sort order, the version router can restore the old behaviour for pinned keys, and the change is rolled back by a flag.

failures.scenario: A paying customer passes its monthly quota on the last day of the month
failures.impact: A hard cutoff would stop their checkout, and billing then loses a customer over a few thousand calls.
failures.answer: Paid plans have a soft limit: the app keeps working, an overage is billed or the plan is upgraded in one click, and the account owner gets alerts at 80% and 100%. Free plans are blocked with a clear 429 body that says how to upgrade. The rate limit, which protects the platform, stays strict.

failures.scenario: A big customer is still on a version on its sunset date
failures.impact: Switching the version off will stop their business, and extending it for everyone defeats the policy.
failures.answer: The usage data found them months earlier, and the brownouts reminded them. The sunset date can be extended for that one key, with a contract and an end date, by an override in the version router, while everyone else is switched off on schedule.

alternatives.title: How versions are named

options.name: In the URL, such as /v2/payments
options.pro: Visible, easy to test in a browser and to route
options.con: Only large, whole-API versions fit, so developers face rare, big upgrades

options.name: In a header, with date-based versions
options.pro: Small frequent changes, and a key pinned to the date it signed up
options.con: Hidden from casual readers, and every date must be kept working

options.name: No versions, only additive changes
options.con: Mistakes stay forever, and the API only grows

alternatives.pick: A date-based version pinned per key, and a major URL version only for a full redesign.

alternatives.title: What happens at the quota

options.name: Hard cutoff
options.con: Production traffic stops at an unpredictable moment

options.name: Soft limit with overage
options.pro: Customers are never stopped, and the platform earns more
options.con: Surprise bills, and abuse must be limited by the rate limit

options.name: Throttle to a lower rate
options.pro: Keeps apps alive but slows them down
options.con: Hard to explain, and still a degraded customer experience

alternatives.pick: Soft for paid plans with alerts, hard for free plans.

alternatives.title: How the SDK is made

options.name: Generated from the OpenAPI description
options.pro: Always in step with the API, in many languages
options.con: Generic style, and wrapper code is needed for niceties

options.name: Written by hand
options.con: Slow to update, and drifts from the API

options.name: Generated core with a thin hand-written layer
options.pro: Correct by construction and still friendly

alternatives.pick: Generated core with a thin hand-written layer for the main languages.

alternatives.title: Authentication for the API

options.name: Static API keys
options.con: Long-lived, so a leak is serious

options.name: OAuth tokens
options.pro: Short-lived and scoped, with users granting access to apps
options.con: More to build, and harder for a first call

options.name: Signed requests
options.pro: The secret never leaves the client
options.con: Hard to try with curl, and clock problems

alternatives.pick: Keys for a developer's own account, and OAuth for apps acting on behalf of other users.
